questions.q: In which year was the Delhi Sultanate established, and who was its first ruler?
questions.a: The Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 CE by Qutb-ud-din Aibak. If a student answers Mahmud of Ghazni (early 11th century) or Muhammad of Ghur, they confuse earlier invaders and raid campaigns with the formal institutional foundation of an independent Indian sultanate.

questions.q: Why did the establishment of the Sultanate in 1206 CE mark a fundamental break from the earlier invasions of Mahmud of Ghazni?
questions.a: Mahmud of Ghazni led seasonal military expeditions primarily to loot wealth and finance his Central Asian empire without establishing permanent political rule in India; in contrast, the rulers of 1206 CE settled permanently in India, severed political dependence on Central Asia, and created local administrative institutions. If a student says the difference was merely the size of their armies or religion, they fail to grasp the conceptual difference between economic plunder and sovereign territorial state-building.

questions.q: A historian finds a 13th-century coin minted in Delhi bearing the title 'Sultan' alongside an inscription recognizing the Caliph of Baghdad. How does this demonstrate a strategy for establishing political legitimacy in early medieval India?
questions.a: Minting coins locally with Islamic imperial titles while invoking the distant Abbasid Caliph gave the early Sultans dual legitimacy: practical economic sovereignty within north India and symbolic religious-legal authority recognized across the wider Islamic world, discouraging rivals from treating them merely as rebellious regional military generals. If a student suggests it means the Caliph of Baghdad directly ruled Delhi, they misunderstand symbolic medieval Islamic sovereignty versus actual regional political autonomy.

questions.q: Analyze two geographical and political reasons why Delhi proved to be a more strategic capital for an all-India empire than Lahore or Ghazni.
questions.a: Geographically, Delhi sits at the narrow corridor between the Aravalli hills and the Yamuna River, commanding the fertile agricultural plains of the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and controlling prime east-west trade routes. Politically, locating the capital at Delhi insulated the Sultanate from immediate Central Asian and Mongol border conflicts in the northwest while providing a forward base to launch military campaigns into central and southern India. If a student mentions only defensive walls or religious reasons, they overlook the economic, geographical, and geopolitical factors of imperial state-building.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The early Delhi Sultanate survived because of its military strength alone." Is this statement adequate? Justify your stance with historical evidence.
questions.a: The statement is inadequate. While military dominance (cavalry tactics, fortresses) was vital for conquest, the Sultanate's survival depended equally on administrative adaptation: integrating local village revenue collectors (*khuts*, *muqaddams*), implementing the *iqta* system to pay commanders without bankrupting the central treasury, and negotiating with regional elites. Pure military force without revenue administration and political compromise would have caused immediate collapse under constant local rebellions. If a student simply agrees that brute military force was everything, they miss the institutional mechanisms required for state stability.

questions.q: Construct a brief conceptual framework showing how a foreign military command transforms into a permanent territorial state. Outline three essential stages with examples from the early Sultanate period.
questions.a: A strong answer must outline: (1) **Military conquest and garrisoning** (e.g., Ghurid victories at Tarain, setting up garrison towns / *iqtas*), (2) **Political independence and institutionalization** (e.g., Aibak declaring sovereignty in 1206 CE, establishing local courts and coinage), and (3) **Consolidation and bureaucratic governance** (e.g., stabilizing borders, integrating local revenue administration, and securing recognition). If a student only lists names of kings without structural stages, they have not demonstrated the ability to conceptualize state-building processes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Delhi Sultanate was a major medieval Islamic polity based in Delhi that ruled extensive parts of the Indian ______ from 1206 to 1526 CE, established following the military campaigns of Muhammad of Ghur and formally founded by his general, Qutb-ud-din Aibak, who inaugurated the Mamluk (Slave) Dynasty.
Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ near the Qutb Minar complex in Mehrauli, South Delhi, looking at stone towers built more than 800 years ago.
Fill in the blank: We begin by connecting to what you learned earlier about the Second Battle of Tarain (______ CE), which broke Rajput dominance in northern India.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Students can explain how and why the Delhi Sultanate was established in 1206 CE, distinguish between seasonal raid campaigns and territorial conquest/state-building, and analyze the political challenges faced by its earliest rulers in shifting the seat of power to Delhi.
